DILG • Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA corner Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City LIGAYA H. HERALDO http: //www.dilg.com.ph JAN 31 2020 D'LG OPINION NO. S, Vice-Mayor, Municipality of Vinzons, Province of Camarines Norte Dear Vice-Mayor Heraldo: This has reference to the letter you sent dated 06 November 2018, seeking this Department's clarification and legal opinion on the propriety of leasing a portion of the municipal hall as commercial stalls to private individuals. In the said letter, a brief background of the facts are as follows: The Municipal Hall Building is surrounded by various commercial stalls being leased to private stallholders in the municipality; • The stalls are located within the lot identified as Municipal Hall Site; • Prior to the change of administration in 2016, the stallholders were awarded a lease contract by then Mayor Agnes D. Ang without securing an authorization from the Sangguniang Bayan; Upon expiration of the lease contracts, the incumbent Local Chief Executive (LCE) has not renewed the same pending authorization from the Sangguniang Bayan (SB); The SB issued Resolution No. 14-2017 ("Resolution Strongly Opposing the On-going Construction of the Multipurpose Building within the Municipal Building Compound, Beside the Barangay Hall of this Municipality") raising the concern that the project was implemented without prior consultation or approval by the SB; • The multi-purpose hall was constructed within the Municipal Hall Site and was then converted commercial stalls and leased to private individuals; • All of these commercial stalls are within the Municipal Hall Site and are currently devoted to commercial use. Under this premise arose the request for clarification regarding the propriety of leasing these commercial stalls.

Accordingly, the queries submitted for this Department's legal opinion are hereunder quoted in verbatim: 1. Whether or not it is legally permissible to devote a portion of the Municipal Hal/ Site for commercial purposes; 2. Whether or not the Local Government Unit may validly enter into a contract of lease with private individuals over these commercia/ stalls; and 3. If the answer in the preceding question is in the negative, what measures if any, should the local government undertake to rectify this mistake; Considering that the first two questions are interrelated, this Department deems it appropriate to tackle the issues in one discussion. At the outset, it is imperative to cite the provisions of Republic Act No. 7160 otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, as amended (LGC) which empowers the local government units (LGUs) to derive income from its properties, to wit: "SECTION 18. Power to Generate and Apply Resources. — Local government units shall have the power and authority to... xxx xxx xxx; acquire, develop, lease encumber, alienate, or otherwise dispose of real or personal property held bv them in their proprietary capacity and to apply their resources and assets for productive, developmental, or welfare purposes, in the exercise or furtherance of their governmental or proprietary powers and functions and thereby ensure their development into self- reliant communities and active participants in the attainment of national goals. " SECTION 22. Corporate Powers. — (a) Every local government unit, as a corporation, shall have the following po wers: (c) Unless otherwise provided in this Code, no contract may be entered into by the local chief executive in behalf of the local government unit without prior authorization by the sanggunian concerned. A legible copy of such contract shall be posted at a conspicuous place in the provincial capitol or the city, municipal or barangay hall. "

The afore-quoted provisions leave no doubt that prior authorization from the Sangguiniang Bayan is necessary in order for the Local Chief Executive to enter into contracts in behalf of the municipality. In addition, this Department would like to invite your attention to the case of The Province of Zamboanga del Norte v. City of Zamboanga5, wherein the Supreme Court made a pronouncement as to two established norms to determine the classification of the properties. According to the High Court, properties for the free and indiscriminate use of everyone are classified under the Civil Code6 as property for public use, while all other properties are patrimonial in nature. In contrast, under the Municipal Corporations Law, to be considered public property, it is enough that a property is held and devoted to a governmental purpose, such as local administration, public education, and public health. However, the Court clarified that the classification of properties in the municipalities, other than those for public use, as patrimonial under Article 424 of the Civil Code, is "without prejudice to the provisions of special laws," holding that the principles obtaining under the Law of Municipal Corporations can be considered as "special laws". Hence, it is essential to distinguish between property for public use and patrimonial property for the reason that property of the provinces, cities, and municipalities for public use are outside the commerce of man, and cannot be leased, donated, sold, or be the object of any contract, except insofar as they may be the subject of repairs or improvements and other incidental things of similar character. On the other hand, patrimonial property is property owned by the state in its private or proprietary capacity which may be an object of ordinary contract. In administering the patrimonial property of municipalities, the municipal council occupies, for most purposes, the position of a board of directors of a private corporation. (Mendoza v. De Leon, G.R. No. L-9596, February 11, 1916) Correspondingly, the municipal hall building is of public dominion as it is devoted for public service. Note however that the actual municipal hall is entirely different from the lot/site wherein it is situated. Hence, following the principles proclaimed by the Supreme Court in The Province of Zamboanga del Norte v. City of Zamboanga case, if the Civil Code will be applied, this Department is of the view that the lot is of patrimonial property since it is not available to the public compared to the actual municipal hall building. Also, in applying the Municipal Corporation Law, this Department is still of the view that the lot is patrimonial property since it is not entirely held and devoted to a governmental purpose. GR No. L-24440, Mar. 28, 1968 6 Art. 423. The property Of provinces, cities, and municipalities is divided into property for public use and patrimonial property. Art. 424. Property for public use, in the provinces, cities, and municipalities, consist of the provincial roads, city streets, municipal streets, the squares, fountains, public waters, promenades, and public works for public service paid for by said provinces, cities, or municipalities. All other property possessed by any of them is patrimonial and shall be governed by this Code, without prejudice to the provisions of special laws."

In view of the foregoing, this Department is of the considered view that an LGU may devote a portion of the Municipal Hall Site for commercial purposes and may validly enter into a contract of lease with private individuals over these properties provided that the properties are held by the Municipality (I) in a proprietary capacity and that there is (2) prior authorization from the Sanggunian Bayan. In relation to your third query, there is nothing yet to be rectified since it was mentioned in your letter that the Local Chief Executive has not renewed the contract of lease pending the issuance of authorization from the Sangguniang Bayan in accordance with the provisions of the LGC. We hope to have addressed your concern accordingly. Thank you. Very tru y y rs, EDU DO ANO Secretary COPY FURNISHED: ATTY. ANTHONY C. NUYDA, CESO 111 Regional Director DILG - Region V Regional Office NO. 5, Rizal St., Legazpi City LLLS/32
